cards.body: Check `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`: no quotes or spaces, not revoked, from the right workspace.

cards.title: Cut-off answers or quizzes

items.text: LLMs predict tokens; tokens drive cost, limits and speed
The API is stateless: send and trim the history yourself
Errors, retries, refusals, costs and budgets

scenes.question: Why do output tokens matter more for cost than many beginners expect?
options: They usually cost several times more than input tokens
They don't count toward the context window
scenes.explain: On Claude Opus 5.5, output tokens cost $20 per million vs $4 for input: five times more. Ask for concise answers.

scenes.question: What does `stop_reason == "max_tokens"` tell you?
options: The reply was cut off at your limit and may be incomplete
The context window is full of history
scenes.explain: The reply hit `max_tokens` and stopped, possibly mid-sentence or mid-JSON. Raise the limit or ask for less.

scenes.question: A chat app's bot forgets everything said earlier. What's the most likely bug?
options: The app doesn't send the earlier messages with each request
scenes.explain: The API is stateless. The app must send the history (and store each reply) on every request.

scenes.question: Which errors are worth retrying automatically?
scenes.explain: Rate limits, server errors and network failures can recover. The Anthropic SDK retries them twice by default, with backoff.

scenes.question: What does `client.messages.parse(..., output_format=Quiz)` give you?
options: Plain text you must parse yourself
A guarantee the quiz is factually correct
scenes.explain: You get a validated object that matches the schema. Structure is guaranteed, **truth is not**: facts still need checking.

captions.text: Welcome back.
Explanations work.
Now we add quizzes as structured output, a chat mode with trimmed history, and the
command line that ties it together.
Then we'll run the full demo, look at the tests, and finish the module.
A question has its text, exactly four options, the index of the correct option, and
an explanation of why it's right.
A quiz is a topic plus a list of questions.
This one class becomes the JSON schema the model must follow.
Make quiz fills in the request: write N multiple-choice questions about a topic.
It calls parse with output format set to Quiz, so the reply is constrained to the
schema.
Quizzes need more care than explanations, so we use medium effort, and a generous
max tokens.
If the reply somehow doesn't fit the schema, for example three options instead of
four, the SDK's validation raises a pydantic validation error, and we turn it into
one clear message.
Finally, if the quiz was cut off by max tokens, we refuse to return a half-finished
quiz, and suggest asking for fewer questions.
For trimming, a quick local estimate is good enough: about four characters per
token.
When you need an exact number, use the token counting endpoint instead.
A chat session holds the history list and a token budget for it.
Trim drops the oldest user and assistant pair while the history is over budget,
exactly the rule from lesson three.
It always keeps at least the latest exchange.
Send appends the question, trims, and calls the model with the whole history.
If the call fails, it removes the unanswered question, so the history never ends up
with two user turns in a row.
Then the reply is stored.
For explain, the on text callback prints each piece immediately.
The footer with tokens and cost goes to standard error, so it never mixes into
output you save or pipe.
Quiz prints the questions with letters, optionally saves the JSON, and grades your
answers if you pass them.
Chat reads one message per line from standard input, so it works interactively, and
from a file for demos and tests.
And main builds the settings, the client, and the assistant, and turns any study
error into one clean line and exit code one, just like Module 1's toolkit.
A two-question quiz, graded.
These are the fake API's placeholder questions, but they went through exactly the
same structured output path: schema, parsing, and validation.
And a chat with two messages piped in.
Look at the second reply: the request carried two earlier messages.
That's our history at work.
The tokens command uses the counting endpoint.
Offline, it's labelled as an estimate.
Now the failure paths.
A single rate limit: the SDK retries automatically and the explanation still
arrives.
Three rate limits in a row exhausts the two retries, and we get one clear error
line, not a traceback.
And a refusal is reported plainly too.
The tests use the fake API as a test double.
This one checks that the explanation arrived in pieces, that the pieces add up to
the final text, and, by inspecting what the fake received, that the request really
was streamed, with fallbacks, and with the right prompt.
This test proves max tokens truncation is detected.
And these two test the SDK's real retry behaviour: two failures then success makes
three requests, and three rate limits in a row becomes our clean error.
Twenty-three tests, all passing, with no key and no network.
A conftest fixture also removes any real key from the environment during tests, so
they can never cost you money.
And mypy is happy with every type hint, including the SDK's own types.
If your key is rejected, check the environment variable: no stray quotes or spaces,
not revoked, and from the right workspace.
If you expected real answers but see offline mode, Python can't see the key.
Set it in the same terminal session.
Repeated rate limits mean you're sending too fast for your account's limits.
Slow down, or allow more retries.
And for cut-off answers, raise max tokens, or ask for less.
